definition: Generative literature is poetry or fiction that is automatically generated, often using computers.
details: It is a genre of electronic literature, and also related to generative art. John Clark's Latin Verse Machine (1830–1843) is probably the first example of mechanised generative literature, while Christopher Strachey's love letter generator (1952) is the first digital example. With the large language models (LLMs) of the 2020s, generative literature is becoming increasingly common.

explainer.lead: Generative literature is poetry or fiction produced automatically, often by a computer. It connects literary writing with electronic literature and generative art, and its history stretches from a nineteenth-century verse machine to modern large language models.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a story-making machine: you set it going, and it produces a poem or story without a person writing every sentence. People were making machines like this long before modern chatbots, including one that generated Latin verse and an early computer program that wrote love letters.
tiers.practitioner: This can be implemented as automatic text generation with a computer program or a large language model, with poetry or fiction as the intended output. The generating setup may vary, but the defining feature is that the literary text is produced automatically rather than written in full directly by a person.

explainer.example: Running Christopher Strachey's love letter generator in 1952 made a computer automatically produce a love letter. This is a concrete early digital example of generative literature.

explainer.intuition: Instead of a person composing every sentence, a mechanism or program generates the text. When the result is poetry or fiction, it falls within generative literature.
howItWorks: Choose poetry or fiction as the desired kind of output.
Set up an automatic generator, such as a mechanism, computer program, or LLM.
Run the generator to produce literary text.
Read or use the resulting generated poem or fiction.
explainer.whyItMatters: It shows that automatic literary creation is not just a recent LLM phenomenon: mechanised and digital examples appeared long before the 2020s. It also forms a point of connection between electronic literature and generative art.
misconceptions: It is not limited to modern LLMs; mechanised examples date back to the nineteenth century.
Electronic literature is broader: generative literature specifically concerns automatically generated poetry or fiction.
